title: Surface Area of Pyramids, Cones and Spheres

findings.finding: The example substitutes 32 mm without connecting it to the labelled 64 mm base edge.
findings.breakdown: Students must infer which horizontal distance the internal triangle needs and why that distance is half the square's side.
findings.checked: The preceding definitions identify the two heights, and the static model states Pythagoras' theorem. Neither states the calculation producing 32 mm.
findings.assumptions: Students know elementary properties of a square; the new decision is selecting the distance within the solid.

repair.proposal: Before substitution, add: 'The distance from the centre of the square base to the midpoint of an edge is 64 ÷ 2 = 32 mm.'

findings.doneWhen: The geometric meaning and origin of 32 mm are stated before its use.

findings.finding: The opening does not rehearse setting up and solving numerical Pythagoras equations for either the hypotenuse or a shorter side.
findings.breakdown: Students must retrieve the equation-solving method while learning to select right triangles inside solids. Displaying the theorem does not rehearse those decisions.
findings.checked: There is no earlier topic or opening review. The static formula and triangle identify the sides but contain no retrieval questions.
findings.assumptions: Pythagoras' theorem is prior knowledge. A calculator may be used; calculator arithmetic is not the missing component.

repair.proposal: Before the solid examples, add: '(a) A right triangle has perpendicular sides 6 cm and 8 cm. Write an equation and find its hypotenuse x. (b) A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 mm and one shorter side 5 mm. Write an equation and find the other side y. (c) A right triangle has hypotenuse 7 m and one shorter side 3 m. Find the other side z in exact surd form.' Answers: x² = 6² + 8², x = 10 cm; y² + 5² = 13², y = 12 mm; z = √40 m. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse forming the equation, isolating the unknown square and taking the positive root before working within solids.

findings.finding: The later sideways-cone question repeats the complete numerical task from guided practice.
findings.breakdown: Both tasks give diameter 6 cm and perpendicular height 10 cm and require the slant height. Changing the unknown's name does not provide a different task.
findings.checked: The stems, givens, orientation and required calculation match. Neither task states a retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.assumptions: No explicit instructional purpose for the unchanged repetition is supplied.

repair.proposal: Change p5-q1-f to a sideways cone with diameter 8 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm. Retain the request for slant height l. Answer: √97 cm.

findings.doneWhen: The later copy retains its structure and representation with different measurements.

findings.finding: The surface-area example combines rectangle and triangle area formulas without an opening review of either.
findings.breakdown: Students who cannot retrieve these formulas must recover them while learning to organise the faces of a pyramid.
findings.checked: The preceding heights topic and its exercise practise Pythagoras and height identification, not area formulas. This topic has no review.
findings.assumptions: Rectangle and triangle areas are prior knowledge from earlier years or the separately listed area booklets. A calculator is assumed.

repair.proposal: Before p6-information-text, add: '(a) Find the area of a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm. (b) Find the area of a triangle with base 8 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm. (c) Find the combined area of two triangles, each with base 5 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm.' Answers: 40 cm², 24 cm², 35 cm². Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students retrieve and use both area formulas before the combined surface-area calculation.

findings.finding: Part c changes from supplied face heights on rectangular nets to an equilateral triangular net requiring an unshown altitude construction.
findings.breakdown: The base shape, face grouping and height-finding decisions change together. Students must construct an altitude, halve an edge and apply Pythagoras before calculating four triangular areas.
findings.checked: All preceding surface-area examples and parts supply face heights. Earlier Pythagoras teaching does not model constructing the altitude of an equilateral triangle. No later part supplies that bridge.
findings.assumptions: Pythagoras is available from the preceding topic; the geometric construction is the missing bridge.

repair.proposal: Add beside part c: “Draw the perpendicular height of one triangular face. It divides the opposite 10 cm side into two 5 cm lengths. Use Pythagoras to find this height, then find the area of all four congruent faces.”

findings.doneWhen: The construction connects the task to the taught Pythagoras method while students perform the calculations.

findings.finding: Compare pyramids with the same square base and doubled face heights.
findings.breakdown: The comparison distinguishes the unchanged base contribution from the doubled triangular contribution.
findings.checked: The original area is 432 cm². With face heights 24 cm, the area is 144 + 576 = 720 cm², which is 144 cm² less than twice the original.
findings.assumptions: Uses only the face-area method taught in this topic.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts to p7-q1-a: (i) A second pyramid has the same 12 cm square base, but each triangular face has perpendicular height 24 cm. Find its total surface area. Answer: 720 cm². (ii) Explain why this is less than twice the original total surface area. Answer: The triangular areas double, but the 144 cm² base area stays unchanged.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the original pyramid and separates the calculation from the explanation.

findings.finding: The rectangular-pyramid example does not state how its 8 cm and 6 cm horizontal legs follow from the base dimensions.
findings.breakdown: The cross-sections supply the resulting lengths without modelling which base dimension produces each one. Students can copy the substitutions without learning that selection.
findings.checked: Earlier work uses square bases. The annotated solid and cross-sections identify the selected lengths but contain no written connection to halving the respective rectangular dimensions.
findings.assumptions: Students know the earlier square-base construction; the rectangular case introduces two different offsets.

repair.proposal: Before the equations, add: 'For x, the horizontal distance from the base centre to the midpoint of the 12 cm edge is 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm. For y, the distance to the midpoint of the 16 cm edge is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.'

findings.doneWhen: Each horizontal leg is explicitly connected to its original base dimension and corresponding face.

findings.finding: The example substitutes radius 9 cm without connecting it to the labelled diameter 18 cm.
findings.breakdown: The worked solution introduces a different measurement without stating the geometric conversion required before substitution.
findings.checked: Earlier practice includes diameter-to-radius conversion, but this example contains no line connecting its own labelled diameter to the substituted radius.
findings.assumptions: The standard requires a written connection when a worked example substitutes a radius for a labelled diameter.
findings.doneWhen: The labelled diameter is explicitly connected to the substituted radius.

findings.finding: The cone topic does not rehearse circle area or recognising and converting a diameter before its worked examples use them.
findings.breakdown: Students must retrieve the circular-base calculation and radius selection while learning the additional cone-area term.
findings.checked: The immediately preceding pyramid topic and exercise do not rehearse circles. Diameter conversion occurs in the older heights topic, but there is no cone opening review.
findings.assumptions: Circle area is prior knowledge from earlier learning or the separately listed circle-area booklet. A calculator is assumed.

repair.proposal: Before the cone definition, add: '(a) Write the formula for the area of a circle. (b) A circle has diameter 18 cm. Find its radius. (c) Find the area of a circle with diameter 10 cm, leaving your answer in terms of π.' Answers: πr²; 9 cm; 25π cm².

findings.doneWhen: A brief opening review rehearses circle area and diameter-to-radius conversion.

findings.finding: In the supplied order, the inscribed-square pyramid task immediately follows direct cone substitution.
findings.breakdown: The task simultaneously introduces an inscribed square, its diagonal relationship and linked exact-length and area calculations before the intervening multistep practice.
findings.checked: The practice array places p17-q10 immediately after p14-q1. Its separate parts provide useful scaffolding, but p14-q2 through p17-q9 provide the existing progression into linked calculations.
findings.assumptions: The supplied practice order is the encounter order, as stated in the candidate.

repair.proposal: Move the complete p17-q10 block to immediately after p17-q9, retaining all its parts.

findings.doneWhen: The inscribed-pyramid task follows the intervening multistep cone practice.

findings.finding: The curved-area questions require selecting πrl before the teaching identifies that term as curved surface area.
findings.breakdown: Students may substitute the given curved area into the total-area formula and incorrectly subtract a base area.
findings.checked: The initial formula labels dimensions, not area contributions. All initial examples calculate totals. The investigation identifies the curved term only after the exercise. Both q4 and q5 require the distinction.
findings.assumptions: Curved cone area is new in this topic; equation solving is prior knowledge.

repair.proposal: Beside the initial formula, add: “Base area = πr²; curved surface area = πrl. Total surface area is their sum.”

findings.doneWhen: Both terms are identified before students select a formula for a given curved area.

findings.finding: Hold radius fixed while increasing slant height to expose the fixed base contribution and changing curved contribution.
findings.breakdown: Equal increases in slant height produce equal increases in total area when radius stays fixed.
findings.checked: Using A = πr² + πrl gives 21π, 27π and 33π cm² for the run, and 44π cm² for the unpatterned follow-up. All cones have slant height greater than radius.
findings.assumptions: Use a calculator and the existing instruction to round to two decimal places.

repair.proposal: After p14-q1-c, add the single instruction: 'Predict how the answers will change before calculating.' Add parts under the existing surface-area instruction: '(d) r = 3 cm, l = 4 cm. (e) r = 3 cm, l = 6 cm. (f) r = 3 cm, l = 8 cm. (g) Diameter 8 cm, l = 7 cm.' Answers: 65.97 cm², 84.82 cm², 103.67 cm², 138.23 cm². Keep the orientation fixed through d–f.

findings.doneWhen: Three consecutive parts vary only slant height and are followed by the unpatterned part.

findings.finding: The hemisphere example substitutes 1.75 m without connecting it to the labelled diameter 3.5 m.
findings.breakdown: The worked calculation introduces its radius without stating how it follows from the diagram.
findings.checked: Earlier cone practice rehearses this conversion, but the hemisphere example itself contains no connecting line. Prior familiarity does not supply the missing worked decision required by the standard.
findings.assumptions: Calculator use does not supply the geometric choice of radius.
findings.doneWhen: The labelled diameter is explicitly connected to the substituted radius.

findings.finding: Compare open hemisphere, closed hemisphere and sphere areas at a fixed radius.
findings.breakdown: The comparison connects the coefficients 2, 3 and 4 to the surfaces included.
findings.checked: For radius 3 cm, the areas are 18π, 27π and 36π cm². A closed hemisphere of diameter 10 cm has area 75π cm². All formulas are taught in p19.

repair.proposal: Broaden p20-q2's instruction to include spheres and closed hemispheres. Add: “Predict how the areas will compare before calculating.” Append (d) open hemisphere, radius 3 cm: 56.55 cm²; (e) closed hemisphere, radius 3 cm: 84.82 cm²; (f) sphere, radius 3 cm: 113.10 cm². Follow with (g) closed hemisphere, diameter 10 cm: 235.62 cm².

findings.doneWhen: The comparison holds radius and units fixed and varies only the included surfaces, followed by an unpatterned part.

findings.finding: Vary the cylinder diameter while retaining the hemisphere and cylinder height.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up exposes why the cylinder top and exposed annulus together retain the hemisphere's original flat-face area.
findings.checked: With hemisphere radius 3 cm and cylinder height 3 cm, total exposed area is 27π + 6πr. Cylinder radii 1 cm and 3 cm give 33π and 45π cm². At radius 3 cm the annulus has zero area, and the cylinder top supplies the full 9π cm².
findings.assumptions: Uses the same cylinder-area and exposed-surface methods required by the existing question.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts to p23-q9: (a) If the cylinder diameter becomes 2 cm and its height remains 3 cm, find the total surface area to 1 d.p. Answer: 103.7 cm². (b) If its diameter becomes 6 cm and its height remains 3 cm, find the total surface area to 1 d.p. Answer: 141.4 cm². (c) Explain why the cylinder top and exposed flat part of the hemisphere have combined area 9π cm² in all three versions. Answer: The cylinder top replaces an equal area covered at the join.

findings.doneWhen: Each follow-up part asks one question and retains the original composite-solid context.

findings.finding: Extend the existing pyramid question to connect its perpendicular height, face slant height and lateral edge.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up combines the two right triangles studied in the topic.
findings.checked: The face slant height is √(85² − 36²) = 77 mm. The perpendicular height is √(77² − 36²) = √4633 mm. Both constructions use methods available by the topic's end.
findings.assumptions: The follow-up is optional and retains the existing right square pyramid.

repair.proposal: After p5-q2-b, add: '(i) Find the perpendicular height of this pyramid in exact surd form. (ii) List the perpendicular height, face slant height and side edge from shortest to longest.' Answers: (i) √4633 mm; (ii) √4633 mm < 77 mm < 85 mm.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts use the existing pyramid and distinguish the three lengths.

findings.finding: Use the recovered pyramid dimensions to compare the effect of doubling perpendicular height.
findings.breakdown: The comparison distinguishes perpendicular height from the slant height that controls triangular-face area.
findings.checked: The original base side is 42 m and its slant height is 35 m. With perpendicular height 56 m, the new slant height is √3577 m and total area is 1764 + 84√3577 ≈ 6787.9 m².
findings.assumptions: Use a calculator for the requested rounded answer and retain the right square-pyramid interpretation.

repair.proposal: After p12-q8, add: '(b) A second right square pyramid has the same base area and perpendicular height 56 m. Find its surface area to the nearest square metre. (c) Is its triangular-face area twice that of the original pyramid? Explain why using the two slant heights.' Answers: (b) 6788 m²; (c) No. The slant heights are 35 m and √3577 m ≈ 59.8 m, so the triangular-face area is multiplied by about 1.71.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up uses the original dimensions and compares the two slant heights.

findings.finding: The frustum introduces several planning decisions together after the additive joined-cones task.
findings.breakdown: Students must reconstruct the complete cone's height, find two slant heights, subtract curved areas and add both circular ends. Earlier questions do not bridge this subtractive decomposition.
findings.checked: Individual slant-height calculations and inverse cone-area work precede this question. The earlier pyramid frustum supplies its face height and can be calculated face by face; it does not model subtracting cone surfaces. Later parts return to additive composites.
findings.assumptions: Pythagoras and basic composite surface area are available. A calculator is assumed; the jump concerns planning rather than arithmetic.

repair.proposal: Add to p16-q8-b: 'Treat the curved surface as a complete cone with a smaller cone removed. Find the complete cone's perpendicular height and both slant heights. Subtract the smaller curved area from the larger curved area, then add the two circular end areas.'

findings.doneWhen: The question supplies a decomposition route while students still select dimensions and perform the calculations.

findings.finding: Extend the existing radius-6-m sphere question to expose the squared effect of doubling radius.
findings.breakdown: The numerical comparison connects the radius multiplier to the surface-area multiplier.
findings.checked: A radius-12-m sphere has area 576π ≈ 1809.56 m², four times the area 144π of a radius-6-m sphere. Only the taught sphere formula is required.
findings.assumptions: Use a calculator for the rounded area.

repair.proposal: After p20-q1-c, add optional parts: '(d) Find the surface area of a sphere with radius 12 m, correct to two decimal places. (e) How many spheres with radius 6 m have the same combined surface area as one sphere with radius 12 m?' Answers: (d) 1809.56 m²; (e) 4.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up explicitly uses the radius from part a and compares the resulting areas.

contextQuestions.question: Before this booklet, have students been taught to calculate exposed surface area by excluding joining faces, including subtracting a smaller cone's curved area to find a frustum's curved area? Please distinguish ordinary joined solids from frustums: this determines whether p16-q8 needs new teaching; its joined-solid practice then precedes p21-q5.

protectedGroups.observation: A lateral edge must first be converted into a perpendicular face altitude; rectangular bases require separate calculations for their two face widths.
protectedGroups.varies: Square versus rectangular base, orientation, dimensions and integer versus non-integer half-base lengths.
protectedGroups.invariant: The supplied sloping length is a lateral edge, and each face altitude is found using a right triangle within that face.

protectedGroups.observation: Surface area counts exposed prism and pyramid faces while excluding their shared join.
protectedGroups.varies: Prism proportions, dimensions and square versus triangular shared base.
protectedGroups.invariant: A prism is capped by a pyramid and the necessary exterior face heights are supplied.

protectedGroups.observation: The same cone formula applies with radius or diameter givens and different orientations.
protectedGroups.varies: Radius versus diameter, orientation, dimensions and units.
protectedGroups.invariant: A closed cone with supplied slant height.

protectedGroups.observation: The slant height remains the hypotenuse of the radius–height triangle regardless of orientation.
protectedGroups.varies: Orientation and radius versus diameter givens.
protectedGroups.invariant: Find slant height before calculating total surface area.

protectedGroups.observation: The exposed-surface calculation transfers to another set of dimensions.
protectedGroups.invariant: A cone with its circular base inscribed in the top of a square prism.
